title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: The night Levin had spent on the haycock did not pass without leaving its mark. The way he had been running his estate revolted him; it had lost all its appeal. In spite of the magnificent harvest, there had never been — or at least it seemed to him there had never been — so many obstacles and so many quarrels between him and the peasants as that year, and the root of these failures and this hostility was now completely clear to him. The pleasure he had taken in the work itself, the closeness with the peasants that grew out of it, the envy he felt for them and their way of life, the desire to live that way — which that night had been not a daydream but a definite intention, the carrying out of which he had worked through in detail — all of it had so changed his view of the farming he had been doing that he could no longer take his old interest in it, and could not help seeing the ugly relation between himself and the workers that lay underneath. The herd of improved cows like Pava, the whole land plowed and enriched, the nine level fields surrounded by hedges, the two hundred and forty acres heavily manured, the seed sown in drills, and all the rest of it — all of it would have been splendid if only the work had been done for themselves, or for themselves and comrades who shared their feelings. But now he saw clearly (his work on a book about agriculture, in which the laborer was to have been the chief element of husbandry, helped him greatly here) that the kind of farming he was carrying on was nothing but a cruel, stubborn struggle between him and his workers, with on one side — his side — a constant intense effort to remake everything along lines he thought better, and on the other side, the natural order of things. And in this struggle, with enormous expenditure of effort on his side and no effort and not even any intention on the other, he saw that all that was achieved was that the work pleased neither side, and that splendid tools, splendid livestock and land were spoiled to no one's benefit. Worst of all, the energy thrown into this work wasn't merely wasted. Now that the meaning of the system had become clear to him, he couldn't help feeling that the very aim of his energy was unworthy. What was the struggle actually about? He was struggling for every farthing of his share (and he had to — relax for a moment, and he wouldn't have had the money to pay his laborers' wages), while they were only struggling to be allowed to do their work easily and pleasantly — that is, as they were used to doing it. It was in his interests for every laborer to work as hard as possible and stay alert, so as not to break the winnowing machines, the horse rakes, the threshing machines, and to pay attention to what he was doing. What the laborer wanted was to work as pleasantly as possible, with rests, and above all carelessly and heedlessly, without thinking. Levin saw this at every step that summer. He sent the men to mow clover for hay, picking out the worst patches where the clover was overgrown with grass and weeds and useless for seed; again and again they mowed the best acres of clover, justifying themselves with the claim that the bailiff had told them to, and trying to reassure him that it would make splendid hay. But he knew they had done it because those acres were so much easier to mow. He sent out a hay machine for pitching the hay — it broke at the first row because it was dull work for a peasant to sit on the seat in front with the great wings waving above him. And he was told, "Don't trouble yourself, your honor — the womenfolk will pitch it quick enough." The plows were practically useless, because it never occurred to the laborer to raise the share when turning the plow; forcing it around, he strained the horses and tore up the ground, and Levin was begged not to mind. The horses were allowed to wander into the wheat because not a single laborer would agree to be night-watchman, and in spite of orders, the laborers insisted on taking turns at night duty, and Ivan, after working all day, fell asleep, and was very repentant about his lapse, saying, "Do what you will with me, your honor."

They killed three of his best calves by letting them into the clover aftermath without watching their drinking, and nothing would convince the men they had been bloated by the clover; they offered him the consolation that one of his neighbors had lost a hundred and twelve head of cattle in three days. None of this happened because anyone bore Levin or his farm ill will; on the contrary, he knew they liked him, considered him a simple gentleman (their highest praise). It happened simply because all they wanted was to work merrily and carelessly, and his interests were not only foreign and incomprehensible to them but in fatal conflict with their most legitimate claims. Levin had long felt dissatisfied with his own position with regard to the land. He saw where his boat was leaking, but he didn't look for the leak — perhaps he was deceiving himself on purpose. (If he lost faith in his work, nothing would be left to him.) But now he could no longer keep up the deception. Farming the land as he had been doing it had become not just unattractive but revolting to him, and he could take no further interest in it.

Added to all this was the presence, only twenty-five miles away, of Kitty Shtcherbatskaya — whom he longed to see and couldn't see. Darya Alexandrovna Oblonskaya had invited him, when he was over there, to come — to come with the aim of renewing his offer to her sister, who, Dolly hinted, would accept him now. Levin himself had felt, on seeing Kitty Shtcherbatskaya, that he had never stopped loving her; but he could not go to the Oblonskys' knowing she was there. The fact that he had made her an offer and she had refused him had set an insurmountable barrier between them. "I can't ask her to be my wife simply because she can't be the wife of the man she wanted to marry," he told himself. The thought made him feel cold and hostile toward her. "I wouldn't be able to talk to her without a feeling of reproach; I couldn't look at her without resentment; and she'll only hate me all the more for it, as she's bound to. And besides — how can I now, after what Darya Alexandrovna told me, go to see them? Can I keep from showing that I know what she told me? And go magnanimously to forgive her, to take pity on her? Put on a show in front of her of forgiving and condescending to grant her my love?... What possessed Darya Alexandrovna to tell me that? By chance I might have seen her, and then everything would have happened of itself; but as it is, it's out of the question — completely out of the question!"
Darya Alexandrovna sent him a letter asking for a side-saddle for Kitty's use. "I'm told you have a side-saddle," she wrote. "I hope you'll bring it over yourself."

This was more than he could bear. How could a woman with any intelligence, any tact, put her sister in such a humiliating position? He wrote ten notes, tore them all up, and sent the saddle without any reply. To write that he would come was impossible, because he could not come; to write that he could not come because something prevented him, or that he would be away, was worse. He sent the saddle without an answer, with a sense of having done something shameful. He handed over the now-revolting business of the estate to the bailiff and set off the next day to a remote district to see his friend Sviazhsky, who had splendid grouse marshes nearby and had recently written to remind him of a long-standing promise to stay with him. The grouse-marsh in the Surovsky district had long tempted Levin, but he had kept putting the trip off because of his work on the estate. Now he was glad to get away from the Shtcherbatskys' neighborhood, and even more from his farm work — especially on a shooting expedition, which in times of trouble had always been the best consolation.
